title: SK hynix Unveils First HBF Standard Specifications with SanDisk at FMS 2026
event_hint: SK hynix and Sandisk published first open High Bandwidth Flash (HBF) standard specification via OCP at FMS 2026.
problem: AI inference drives surging data volumes; existing memory hierarchy faces simultaneous bandwidth and capacity scalability bottlenecks that neither HBM nor SSDs alone resolve.
mechanism: HBF is a new memory layer positioned between HBM and SSDs: it uses stacked NAND dies to deliver HBM-like high-speed transfer while significantly expanding capacity. The stack comes in 8-high and 16-high NAND die configurations; the host interconnect adopts the UCIe industry standard so HBF can attach to different processor types (GPUs, CPUs). The spec also defines connection interfaces/electrical characteristics, reliability and die-stack packaging guidelines, and software I/O guidelines.

evidence.claim: First HBF standard specification unveiled by SK hynix in collaboration with Sandisk via the Open Compute Project (OCP), positioned as an open industry standard.
evidence.baseline: proprietary technology / no prior open HBF spec
evidence.condition: announced August 4, 2026 at FMS 2026, Santa Clara
evidence.source_locator: Evidence locator: SK hynix Unveils First HBF Standard Specifications with Sandisk ... – Seoul, August 4, 2026

evidence.claim: HBF capacity specifications cover up to 512GB, based on two stack configurations: 8-high and 16-high NAND dies.
evidence.source_locator: Capacity specifications cover up to 512GB based on two stack configurations (8-high and 16-high NAND dies)

evidence.claim: HBF bandwidth is categorized into three grades (Grade1~3), delivering scalable performance from approximately 0.4TB/s to 3.0TB/s.
evidence.source_locator: Bandwidth is categorized into three grades (Grade1~3), delivering scalable performance from approximately 0.4TB/s to 3.0TB/s

evidence.claim: HBF adopts UCIe as the interconnect linking HBF to processors, enabling flexible integration across GPU and CPU processor types.
evidence.source_locator: HBF technology adopts UCIe, an industry standard connection interface, laying the groundwork to flexibly integrate HBF technology across different processor types, including GPUs and CPUs

evidence.claim: The HBF consortium launched in February 2026, about six months before this spec, following the initial standardization partnership with Sandisk in August 2025; Google and Tenstorrent currently participate.
evidence.source_locator: This milestone comes about six months after launching the consortium in February this year, following the initial standardization partnership with Sandisk in August 2025 ... With Google and Tenstorrent currently participating in the HBF consortium

evaluation_context: Announcement-stage standard specification, not a measured product benchmark. No workload, hardware platform, latency, endurance (P/E), write-amplification, or power measurement is exposed in the visible evidence. Capacity (up to 512GB) and bandwidth (~0.4-3.0TB/s across Grade1-3) are specified ranges, not validated system results.
limitations: Evidence is a vendor newsroom announcement of a specification, not independent characterization. No P/E endurance, access latency, write amplification, power draw, cost/bit, or volume-production timeline is visible. Headline summary claims of ~2.5x power-efficiency gain and ~540x capacity vs HBM are not supported by the visible Evidence Pack text and were not recorded as facts. Maturity (sampling vs mass production) is unspecified.
project_relevance: HBF targets the AI inference bandwidth/capacity gap that influences storage-hierarchy and memory-attachment decisions. UCIe-based open standardization matters for processor-agnostic deployment, but the project card requires distinguishing announced specs from sampled or mass-production capability; here only an open specification and consortium status are confirmed.
source_notes: Source is an SK hynix newsroom announcement (vendor primary) loaded as LOCAL_SOURCE; numbers are specification targets, not measured benchmarks.
Discovery summary mentions ~2.5x power-efficiency improvement and ~540x capacity vs HBM, but these statements are absent from the visible Evidence Pack and were treated as unverified claims.

evidence_gaps.question: What is the power-efficiency improvement of HBF versus prior-generation NAND/HBM, and under what workload or measurement condition (the ~2.5x claim needs a baseline)?
What is the HBF capacity comparison basis versus HBM (the ~540x capacity claim) and which HBM generation/stack is the reference?
